# Background Verification for Security Guard Companies and Agencies in India: PSARA Compliance Guide


September 23, 2026


[Shashank Yadav](https://salarybox.in/blog/author/shashank87cc9f270b/)


[No comments yet](https://salarybox.in/blog/background-verification-for-security-guard-companies-and-agencies-in-india-psara-compliance-guide/#respond)


Background verification for security guards in India is both a regulatory requirement under the Private Security Agencies Regulation Act (PSARA) 2005 and a fundamental business necessity because security guards are hired specifically to protect people, property, and assets, a mandate that is meaningless if the guard’s own identity has not been verified against government databases like the Income Tax Department (PAN), Election Commission (Voter ID), and VAHAN/SARATHI (Driving Licence) through platforms like Compose1 Verify.


The irony of the security industry is hard to miss. Companies hire security guards to prevent unauthorized access, protect against theft, and ensure safety. Yet many of these guards are deployed without their own identity being verified beyond a visual check of an Aadhaar photocopy. The person entrusted with protecting a corporate office, a residential complex, a bank branch, or a hospital entrance may themselves be operating under a false identity.


India’s private security industry employs an estimated 9 to 12 million guards deployed across corporate offices, IT parks, residential societies, banks, hospitals, malls, factories, hotels, educational institutions, and government facilities. The industry is regulated by PSARA at the state level, with each state having its own regulatory authority. Despite regulation, verification practices vary wildly from agency to agency, and many deploy guards with minimal or no database verification.


This guide covers the PSARA regulatory framework, why security guard verification is both a legal and business requirement, what checks are needed, how security agencies can implement cost-effective verification at scale, and how client companies can independently verify guards deployed at their sites.


## PSARA 2005: What the Law Requires


### Licensing Requirements


The Private Security Agencies Regulation Act 2005 requires every private security agency to obtain a licence from the Controlling Authority (typically the state Home Department or Police). The licence application must include details of the agency’s principals, its business operations, and its security personnel.


### Personnel Requirements Under PSARA


PSARA and its associated rules specify requirements for security personnel deployed by licensed agencies. These include age requirements (typically 18 to 65 years), physical fitness standards, training requirements (specified hours of training before deployment), and character and antecedent verification.


The character and antecedent verification requirement under PSARA is where background verification becomes a legal obligation. Agencies must verify that guards do not have criminal records and are of suitable character for security work. While the specific verification methods are not prescribed in detail by the central Act (state rules vary), the intent is clear: deploy only verified, suitable individuals in security roles.


### State-Level Variations


Each state implements PSARA through its own rules. Some states have more detailed verification requirements than others. Delhi, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, and other major states have established regulatory frameworks with specific compliance requirements for security agencies. Regardless of state-level specifics, the principle is consistent: security agencies must verify their personnel.


### Penalties for Non-Compliance


Operating without a PSARA licence or deploying personnel who do not meet regulatory requirements can result in licence revocation, fines, and criminal prosecution of the agency’s principals. For an industry built on trust and compliance, losing a PSARA licence effectively shuts down the business.


## Why Security Guard Verification Is Non-Negotiable


### The Guard Is the Security


A security guard is not an accessory to a security system. In most Indian establishments, the guard is the security system. CCTV cameras record events. Access control systems manage entry logs. But the guard is the human decision-maker who decides who enters, who is stopped, who is questioned, and what action is taken during an incident.


If the guard is operating under a false identity, the entire security premise collapses. The person making access decisions for your building, handling your keys, monitoring your CCTV feeds, and patrolling your premises at night is someone you cannot identify. The security guard you hired to prevent unauthorized access is themselves an unauthorized person.


### Guards Have Master Access


Security guards typically have access to areas that no other employee has. Master keys to all offices. Access codes for restricted zones. CCTV monitoring room access. Knowledge of security system blind spots. Knowledge of patrol schedules and when areas are unmonitored.


A guard with malicious intent and a false identity has more information about your security vulnerabilities than any external threat. They know when the CCTV does not cover an area. They know when the patrol gap is longest. They know where valuable assets are stored. And because their identity is fake, they cannot be traced after an incident.


### Client Contracts Depend on Verified Guards


Enterprise clients, especially in BFSI, IT, and multinational corporations, require their security vendors to provide verified guards with documented background checks. During vendor audits, clients request verification records for deployed personnel. A security agency that cannot produce verification documentation for its guards risks losing contracts worth crores.


Having downloadable PDF verification reports from[Compose1 Verify](https://compose1.com/verify/) for every deployed guard provides audit-ready documentation that satisfies client compliance requirements.


### Insurance and Liability


When a security incident occurs at a client site (theft, unauthorized access, assault), the investigation inevitably examines the security arrangements. If the guard on duty was unverified and operating under a false identity, the security agency faces negligent deployment liability, potential insurance claim complications, and criminal liability if the guard was complicit in the incident.


## The Security Guard Verification Framework


### Check 1: PAN Verification (All Guards)


**Why:** Confirms the guard’s identity against the Income Tax Department database. PAN is a foundational identity document that links to the guard’s financial identity, making them traceable through the tax system.


**What it reveals:** Registered name, date of birth, PAN status (active, inactive, deactivated).


**Red flags:** PAN does not exist in the database (fake number). Name does not match what the guard provided (using someone else’s PAN). PAN is deactivated.


**How to do it:** Enter PAN on[Compose1 Verify](https://compose1.com/verify/) . Result in 2 to 3 minutes. Cost: Rs 50 to Rs 200.


### Check 2: Voter ID Verification (All Guards)


**Why:** Cross-confirms identity through an independent government database. The combination of PAN + Voter ID gives you identity confirmation from two separate government agencies, which is significantly stronger than either alone.


**What it reveals:** Registered name, age or date of birth, father’s or husband’s name, constituency details.


**Red flags:** Name or date of birth does not match PAN results. EPIC number returns no result. The guard claims to be from one state but the Voter ID shows a different state (not automatically a red flag, but worth noting for guards claiming local residence).


**Cross-record analysis:** Compose1 Verify automatically compares PAN and Voter ID results. Matching name and date of birth across both databases provides high-confidence identity confirmation. Mismatches are flagged for review.


**How to do it:** Enter Voter ID in the same Compose1 Verify session. Result in 2 to 3 minutes. Cost: Rs 50 to Rs 200 additional.


### Check 3: DL Verification (Guards Who Drive)


**Why:** Many security deployments include mobile patrol in vehicles, escort services, cash-in-transit, and VIP protection that involves driving. Guards assigned to these duties must have valid DLs.


**What it reveals:** Licence validity, authorized vehicle classes, expiry date, suspension status.


**Who needs this:** Guards assigned to mobile patrol vehicles, escort and protection details, cash-in-transit operations, any deployment involving driving.


**How to do it:** Enter DL number and DOB on Compose1 Verify. Result in 2 to 5 minutes. Cost: Rs 50 to Rs 200 additional.


### Check 4: UAN Employment History (Supervisors and Experienced Guards)


**Why:** Security supervisors, shift commanders, and guards hired at premium rates based on claimed experience should have that experience verified. A “supervisor with 10 years at a major security agency” who actually has 1 year as a general guard is underqualified for the leadership role.


**What it reveals:** Formal employment history through EPFO records. Employer names, contribution dates, and member IDs.


**Who needs this:** Security supervisors, shift commanders, guards hired for specialized roles (VIP protection, BFSI deployments), any guard whose wage rate is based on claimed experience.


**How to do it:** Enter UAN on Compose1 Verify. Result in 5 to 30 minutes. Cost: Rs 200 to Rs 500 additional.


## Security Industry Fraud Scenarios


### Scenario 1: The Guard Who Facilitated the Burglary


A security agency deploys a guard at a jewellery showroom in Jaipur. The guard provides PAN and Voter ID photocopies during onboarding. After 3 months, the showroom is burgled during the guard’s night shift. CCTV shows the guard disabling the alarm and opening the back door. Jewellery worth Rs 35 lakh is stolen. Investigation reveals the PAN belongs to a person who lives in another state and has never been to Jaipur. The guard was part of an organized gang that plants members as security guards to facilitate burglaries.


PAN + Voter ID verification through Compose1 Verify would have flagged the identity mismatch (different name or date of birth between documents) before the guard was deployed at the showroom.


### Scenario 2: The Residential Society Guard with a Hidden Past


A security agency deploys a guard at a premium residential society in Mumbai. The guard’s documents appear genuine on visual inspection. After 8 months, a resident reports a break-in. While investigating, the police discover that the guard has a history of theft complaints at two previous housing societies in different cities. He was never caught because he moved to a new city and joined a new agency each time, using slightly different names and document combinations.


While criminal record checks would have caught the theft history, PAN + Voter ID cross-record analysis would have caught the inconsistency in names and documents, preventing deployment before any criminal check was needed.


### Scenario 3: The Cash-in-Transit Guard on a Suspended DL


A security agency provides cash-in-transit services. One of the armed escorts also serves as a backup driver for the armoured van. The guard/driver’s DL was suspended 4 months ago for a traffic violation, but nobody re-verified. During a route change, the guard takes over driving. An accident damages the van and delays the cash delivery. The insurance company discovers the suspended DL and denies the vehicle damage claim. The agency faces Rs 6 lakh in uninsured repairs plus potential loss of the cash-in-transit contract.


Quarterly DL re-verification costing Rs 150 would have caught the suspension before the guard was allowed behind the wheel.


### Scenario 4: The Supervisor with Fabricated Security Experience


A security agency hires a “Senior Supervisor” at Rs 30,000 per month for a high-security corporate deployment. The supervisor claims 12 years at two national security agencies. On-site, the supervisor struggles with basic SOPs: access control protocols, incident reporting, shift management. Client complaints increase. A belated UAN check reveals 18 months at one small local agency and no record of the claimed experience at either national agency.


The agency overpaid and deployed an underqualified supervisor at a high-profile site, risking the client contract.


## Implementing Verification at Scale for Security Agencies


### For Small Security Agencies (50 to 200 Guards)


Small agencies often have a single office manager handling recruitment and administration.


**Process:** The office manager runs verification on Compose1 Verify. When a new guard is recruited, collect PAN and Voter ID numbers on the first day. Run verification before issuing uniform and ID card. Do not deploy unverified guards to any site.


**Time per guard:** 10 to 15 minutes. **Cost per guard:** Rs 100 to Rs 400. **Annual cost for 150 guards (with 30 percent turnover = 195 verifications):** Rs 19,500 to Rs 78,000.


### For Mid-Size Security Agencies (200 to 1,000 Guards)


Mid-size agencies have HR coordinators or recruitment teams.


**Process:** Integrate verification into the recruitment workflow. After interview and selection, run PAN + Voter ID through[Compose1 Verify](https://compose1.com/verify/) before issuing the offer letter. Add DL for mobile patrol and driving assignments. Add UAN for supervisory roles. Maintain a verification register for all deployed guards.


**Annual cost for 500 guards (with 35 percent turnover = 675 verifications):** Rs 67,500 to Rs 270,000.


### For Large Security Agencies (1,000+ Guards)


Large agencies have dedicated HR departments and operate across multiple cities.


**Process:** Centralized verification through Compose1 Verify. Each branch submits new recruit document numbers. Central HR runs verification and issues deployment clearance. Standardized verification ensures consistent quality across all branches and deployments.


**Annual cost for 3,000 guards (with 40 percent turnover = 4,200 verifications):** Rs 420,000 to Rs 1,680,000 (Rs 4.2 to Rs 16.8 lakh).


For context, a large security agency with 3,000 guards generates annual revenue of Rs 30 to Rs 50 crore. The verification cost is 0.03 to 0.06 percent of revenue.


## Client-Side Verification: For Companies Using Security Agencies


### Why Clients Should Verify Guards Independently


You hired a security agency to protect your office. The agency says their guards are verified. But the agency’s verification quality is unknown to you. “Verified” might mean database-checked through a reputable platform, or it might mean “we looked at the Aadhaar photocopy.” You are trusting the agency’s process without knowing what that process is.


Independent verification takes 10 minutes per guard and costs Rs 100 to Rs 400. For the guards who protect your office, your employees, and your assets, this is a negligible investment in confirmed security.


### How to Verify Agency-Deployed Guards


Ask the agency to provide PAN and Voter ID numbers for all deployed guards. Run PAN + Voter ID on Compose1 Verify. For guards who drive patrol vehicles, add DL verification. Download PDF reports and maintain them in your security records.


If the agency objects to providing document numbers, that is itself a red flag. A reputable agency with properly verified guards has no reason to withhold document numbers from a client conducting independent checks.


### Enterprise Client Verification Requirements


For corporate offices, IT parks, BFSI branches, and other enterprise deployments, build guard verification into the security vendor agreement. Specify that all deployed guards must have PAN + Voter ID verification completed through a digital platform before deployment. Require the agency to provide verification reports (or allow you to conduct independent verification). Include quarterly DL re-verification for guards assigned to vehicle-based duties.


## Building a Security Agency Verification Policy


### Recruitment Gate


No guard receives a uniform, ID card, or site assignment until PAN + Voter ID verification is completed through Compose1 Verify. DL verification is additionally required for any guard who will operate a vehicle. This is a zero-exception policy.


### Pre-Deployment Check


Before a guard is deployed to a new client site, verify that their verification records are current (within 6 months for identity, within 3 months for DL). For premium or high-security deployments, re-verify before the assignment.


### Quarterly Re-Verification


DL re-verification every quarter for all guards in vehicle-based roles. Annual PAN re-verification for all guards to catch deactivations and status changes.


### Guard Rotation Verification


When guards are rotated between sites, verify that the replacement guard’s records are current. Do not deploy a guard whose last verification was more than 6 months ago without re-verifying.


### Client Audit Readiness


Maintain a guard verification portfolio for each client site. The portfolio should contain PDF verification reports for every guard currently deployed at that site, a verification status register showing check dates and results, consent forms, and DL re-verification history for vehicle-based guards. This portfolio should be ready for client audit at any time.


### Incident Protocol


When a security incident occurs at any client site, the first documentation step (after ensuring safety) is to pull the deployed guard’s verification file. If the guard was verified, the reports demonstrate due diligence. If the guard was not verified, this becomes a separate compliance issue requiring immediate remediation.


## Cost Analysis: Verification as Business Investment


### Cost of Verification


PAN + Voter ID per guard: Rs 100 to Rs 400. DL per driving guard: Rs 50 to Rs 200 additional. UAN per supervisor: Rs 200 to Rs 500 additional. Quarterly DL re-verification: Rs 50 to Rs 200 per guard.


### Cost of Not Verifying


PSARA licence revocation: Business shutdown. One client contract lost due to unverified guards: Rs 10 lakh to Rs 5 crore in annual revenue. One security incident involving an unverified guard: Rs 5 lakh to Rs 50 lakh in liability. One insurance claim denied due to unverified driver/guard: Rs 5 to Rs 25 lakh. Reputational damage from a publicized incident: Unquantifiable.


### The Business Case


For a 500-guard agency spending Rs 1.5 lakh annually on verification, the cost per guard per year is Rs 300. The monthly billing rate per guard is Rs 15,000 to Rs 25,000. The verification cost is 0.1 to 0.2 percent of the guard’s annual billing. This is not a cost decision. It is a business survival decision.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### Is background verification mandatory for security guards under PSARA?


PSARA requires security agencies to verify the character and antecedents of their personnel. While the Act does not prescribe specific verification platforms, the intent is that agencies must confirm their guards are suitable for security work. Digital identity verification through[Compose1 Verify](https://compose1.com/verify/) satisfies the identity verification component of this requirement. Criminal record checks and police verification may be additionally required depending on state-specific rules.


### How much does it cost to verify security guards?


PAN + Voter ID verification costs Rs 100 to Rs 400 per guard through Compose1 Verify. Adding DL for driving assignments costs Rs 200 to Rs 600 total. No subscription, no contract, no minimum volume. For an agency with 200 guards, annual verification cost (including turnover replacements) is Rs 26,000 to Rs 104,000.


### Should client companies verify guards deployed by security agencies?


Yes. Independent verification takes 10 minutes per guard and costs Rs 100 to Rs 400. Request PAN and Voter ID numbers from the agency and run checks through Compose1 Verify. The security agency was hired to protect your premises. Confirming that the guards themselves have verified identities is a basic due diligence step.


### How often should security guards’ DLs be re-verified?


Quarterly for guards in vehicle-based roles (mobile patrol, escort, cash-in-transit). DLs can expire or get suspended between checks. Quarterly re-verification through Compose1 Verify costs Rs 50 to Rs 200 per guard and takes 2 minutes. After any vehicle incident, immediately re-verify the involved guard’s DL.


### Can small security agencies afford digital verification?


At Rs 100 to Rs 400 per guard, verification is affordable for agencies of any size. A small agency with 50 guards spends Rs 5,000 to Rs 20,000 annually on verification. Compose1 Verify requires no subscription or contract. The cost of losing one client contract due to an unverified guard incident far exceeds the annual verification cost for the entire workforce.


### What if a guard does not have a PAN card?


PAN is increasingly common across employment levels. If a guard does not have PAN, verify their Voter ID as the primary identity check. Require them to apply for PAN within 30 days. For the interim period, Voter ID verification alone provides Election Commission database confirmation of the guard’s identity.


### What records should security agencies maintain for guard verification?


For each guard: PAN verification report (PDF from Compose1 Verify), Voter ID verification report (PDF), DL verification report (for driving guards), UAN verification report (for supervisors), verification date, deployment history, consent form, and re-verification records. Maintain a company-wide verification register and site-specific guard verification portfolios for client audits. Retain records for the duration of employment plus one year.


### How do I verify guards during high-turnover periods?


Security industry turnover can exceed 40 percent annually. Digital verification through Compose1 Verify handles high turnover efficiently. Each verification takes 10 to 15 minutes and costs Rs 100 to Rs 400. One HR coordinator can verify 20 to 30 guards per day. For large-scale recruitment drives, assign additional coordinators. The speed of digital verification means high turnover is a volume challenge, not a time challenge.


## The Guard Protecting Others Must First Be Verified Themselves


Security is built on a single premise: the people you trust to protect you can be trusted. That trust must be verified, not assumed. Every guard deployed at every site should have a government-database-confirmed identity. Every guard who drives should have a verified DL. Every supervisor should have confirmed experience.


Digital verification makes this standard achievable for security agencies of all sizes. The cost is negligible relative to billing. The time is minutes per guard. And the alternative, deploying guards whose identities you cannot confirm, defeats the entire purpose of security.
